segments.text: This evening, the shared table at the Nest holds a map you cannot read with your eyes alone, because every border on it has been traced in string and glued down, red for Britain, blue for France, black for Germany, and in our open newsroom, the whole team has watched one pair of hands move across it all afternoon, stopping again and again at the same town in the northeast, where the card underneath has been pressed thin.
That town is Bawku, and whose hands they are, I will tell you before we close.
My people, what day go on?
I am Kofi, the editor, this is the Gold Coast Palawa, and the price of this third edition, paid as always in data, is about 50 megabytes, a small price for a map Ghana has spent 70 years living with.

If you missed the first two editions, go back for them first, because the king who signed Asante into a colony signed the north into a protectorate on the very same day, and the cocoa farms of our second edition were worked season after season by hands from the very north this story is about.
Page 1, and as the house rule goes, every headline is a question.
Our lead, how did a king's capital end up inside a German colony while most of his kingdom stayed British, and what did a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean have to do with it?
Which Gold Coast soldier fired the first shot of the First World War for the British Empire, and why was it fired in Togoland?
Why did one territory vote in 1956 to join a country that did not yet exist, while four in ten said no?
Why has a town in the upper east slept under curfew since 2021, and tucked in the corner like a classified ad?
Which decision, taken by colonial officers almost a century ago, is still deciding who rules in Bauku tonight?
Start in Berlin, where from November 1884 to February 1885, the powers of Europe agreed the rules for dividing Africa, with not one African in the room.
Germany had already raised its flag east of the Volta that July, and called it Togoland.
Inland, Britain, and Germany both wanted the trading country around Salaga and Yendi, so they declared it a neutral zone.
Which held only until the Germans marched on Yendi, and on the 3rd and 4th of December 1896, the Dagbamba fought them at Ahdibo.
The battle Dagbong still calls Ahdibo Dahli, the day of Ahdibo, before the Germans burned Yendi to the ground.
Then, on the 14th of November 1899, came a deal so strange it belongs on page 1, in a treaty mostly about who would keep the islands of Samoa on the other side of the world.
Britain and Germany also split the neutral zone, so Yendi, the seat of the Yahna, went to Germany, while Sahlaga and the western part of Dagbong stayed British.

On the 26th of September 1901, King Edward VII signed orders in council on one day that made Asante a colony, the ending of our first edition, and created the Northern Territories of the Gold Coast, a protectorate in force from the 1st of January 1902.

The pencil moved again in 1914. Days after Britain declared war on Germany, the Gold Coast Regiment marched into Togoland, and on the 7th of August 1914, near Nwacha, a soldier named Al-Haji Grunshi returned fire on a German-led police patrol.

The first shot fired by a soldier in British service in the whole First World War. Less than three weeks before the colony surrendered, Britain and France then cut Togoland in two, but sliced the idea.
patch

On Wednesday, the 9th of May, 1956, in the first weeks of the rainy season, when the farm roads around Ho and Kapandu turned to red mud, the people of British Togoland queued to decide their future under the eye of a United Nations commissioner, Eduardo Espinoza y Prieto of Mexico.

Some 194,000 people were on the roll, and about 83% of them turned out. The choice on the ballot was blunt. Unite with the Gold Coast, racing towards independence, or remain a United Nations trust territory for now.
Nkrumah's Convention People's Party campaigned for union. The Togoland Congress, strongest among the southern Aive, campaigned against, dreaming of a reunion with the Aive across the French line.
When the count was done, 93,095 people, 58%, had chosen union, and 67,492, 42%, had said no.

The map tells it better than the total. The northern districts of Mahamprusi, Dagomba, and Gonja, together with Bu Em Krachi, voted heavily for union, while the two southern Aive districts, Ho and Kapandu, voted clearly against it.

On the 13th of December, 1956, the United Nations General Assembly approved the union, and on the 6th of March, 1957, British Togoland was born with Ghana, the long eastern strip running from the Volta up through Oti and Dagbong.

Now travel north to Bawku, near the borders with Burkina Faso and Togo, where the question is not which country but which chief, and there are two histories here. This desk will not pretend there is only one.
The Mahamprusi say their people founded the Bawkuskiin in the early 1700s and filled it for two centuries with chiefs sent by the Nayiri at Nalerigu.

In 1952, the Kusasi say they are the people of the land, its first settlers and its custodians, and that the colonial administration placed Mahamprusi chiefs over them, which they date to 1932, because British indirect rule wanted kings to rule through, and the Kusasi had governed themselves without one.
Since independence, government after government has picked up the pen.
In 1958, the Court of Appeal ruled for the Kusasi. After the 1966 coup, a military decree, NLCD 112, handed the skin to the Mahamprusi.
In 1983, PNDC Law 75 returned it to the Kusasi, and in 2003, a Mahamprusi suit at the Supreme Court was withdrawn, which each side reads as its own victory.
In February 2023, the Nayiri enskinned his own Bawku Naba al-Hajji Sayidu Abagre at Nalerigu.
When he arrived in Bawku in October 2024, the shooting returned, and by mid-February 2025, at least 58 people had been killed, children among them.
Asked to mediate the Asante He-Ne-Otumfo Osei Tutu II, presented his report on the 16th of December 2025.
It recognized the Kusasi chief, Asigri Abu-Grago Azoka II, as Bawku Naba, and recommended that Al-Hajji Abagre return to Nale-Rigu or live in Bawku as a private citizen.
The government accepted it and promised a 1 billion CD fund to rebuild Bawku.
The Nayiri rejected it entirely as flawed and biased, and on Christmas Day, the army moved Al-Hajji Abagre out of Bawku.
The 10 at night curfew is still in force, and talks between the two communities, backed by the National Peace Council, go on.
Chale, this desk gives no verdict. It only asks you to notice who was holding the pen each time.
Then, 42% of British Togoland voted to wait. Now, a small movement says the wait never ended.
On the 16th of November, 2019, in Ho, the Homeland Study Group Foundation, led by Charles Kormi Kujorji,
then in his 80s declared a state of Western Togoland, arguing that the 1956 Union was never properly formed.
And at dawn on the 25th of September, 2020, armed men linked to the movement raided the police stations at Mepe and Aveyime and blocked the roads into the Volta.
The state answers that a United Nations plebiscite settled the matter.
The Volta chiefs disowned the declaration, and the courts have jailed members of the armed group.
Yet, in May 2025, the Ekawas court ordered Ghana to pay $75,000 to 30 members, held for long periods without trial.
Both things are true at once. It is not only our story.
In 1947, Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never seen India, was given about five weeks to divide it, and millions were uprooted.
And here is the item in the corner of page one.
Colonial rule drew lines inside the North too, deciding which chiefs would rule which peoples and writing it into law,
so every government since has inherited disputes it could redraw but never erase.
It also decided what the North was for.
Officials sent Northern men south to the mines and cocoa farms and kept schools scarce,
so the North's first secondary school opened in Tahmaleh only in 1951, 75 years after Mafansi Pim in Cape Coast.
In no be small thing, the North was run as a labor reserve, and Boku still lives inside a decision made for it nearly a century ago.
Back at the Nest, the hands on that string map belong to Amo, whom the Nest has decided to call the Discerning.
He carries the name of Anton Wilhelm Amo, a boy taken from near Axim to Germany in the early 1700s,
who grew up to teach philosophy there, and like his namesake, our Amo does not take the world as it is handed to him.
Amo is blind, and he learns a place by touch.
His closest friend at the Nest, whose story is still to come, glued every string down for him,
and he traced each line until his fingers knew Yendi by the knot where the 1899 string swerves away from it.
Late in the evening, he peeled the strings off, one by one, and laid his palm flat on the bear card.
Kwame, the combative, who had argued all day about whose line was right,
ran his hand over it and went quiet, because under every string, the card is one piece.
I will tell you more about Amo in good time.
Before sound, before security systems, I trained in visual arts,
and the first thing any drawing teacher tells you is to sketch in pencil, because pencil can be rubbed out.
Every border in this edition was sketched in pencil in Berlin and London by men who never walked the ground.
Our trouble is that we have been inking over them ever since.
Letters page, and this week's question, asks you to connect.
Bauku's chiefs, the Volta's separatists, and the split of Dagbong,
all trace back to lines drawn before 1914.
So which colonial line still shapes your own town, your family, or your school?
And how?
Tell us in the comments, and I will pin the best answer.
That is the third edition of the Gold Coast Pallava.
Complete, checked, stamped, priced at about 50MB, filed and signed at the Nest 266 Sandpiper Loop,
Onipa Enclave, and dispatched to Accra, to Kumasi, to Boon Kapurugu, to Hafasini, and to the world.
Menas Vimdei.
Make we chat later.
Let's go.
